misconceptions.title: Slope misidentification in inequalities
misconceptions.description: Students identify or interpret slope sign and direction incorrectly when graphing linear inequalities.
misconceptions.consequence: The consequence is shading the wrong half-plane or selecting the wrong boundary orientation, producing an incorrect solution set.

errorsByFrequency.optionSummary: Option shows: solid boundary line, correct shading below
errorsByFrequency.interpretation: Students who selected this likely believe all inequalities use a solid boundary line, or haven't connected the < symbol specifically to a dashed line. The shading is correct — the error is isolated to the line type rule.

errorsByFrequency.optionSummary: Option shows: dashed boundary line, shading above
errorsByFrequency.interpretation: Students who selected this likely believe all inequalities use a solid boundary line, or haven't connected the < symbol specifically to a dashed line. The shading is correct — the error is isolated to the line type rule.

errorsByFrequency.optionSummary: Option shows: dashed boundary line, shading above
errorsByFrequency.interpretation: Students who selected this likely believe all inequalities use a solid boundary line, or haven't connected the < symbol specifically to a dashed line. The shading is correct — the error is isolated to the line type rule.

focusSkill.name: Graphing linear inequalities
focusSkill.description: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

skills.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.
Analyze and solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or nonviable options in a modeling context. *For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods.*

groupFormation.title: Form groups for the activity

groups.label: Group A
groups.description: Students who draw the boundary correctly but occasionally flip the inequality when testing. Focus on practicing the substitution step and verbalizing the inequality direction.

groups.label: Group B
groups.description: Students who misread slope sign from equations or two points. Focus on finding slope from two points and checking sign before drawing.

activity.title: Incorrect Worked examples - Examples to show the class
activity.subtitle: Teacher view shows the error step highlighted. Student view shows the problem clean

examples.label: Example 1
examples.prompt: Graph the solution to y < −1/2 x + 3

steps.text: Draw a dashed line through (0, 3) with slope −1/2.
Since 0 > 3 is false, the student concludes (0, 0) is not a solution and shades the half-plane away from (0, 0).

examples.finalOutcome: Line plotted correctly but shaded the opposite half-plane from the true solution.

examples.label: Example 2

annotation.text: dropped the negative sign; slope should be −2

steps.text: Plot (0, 6) and use slope 2 to plot (1, 8). Draw the line and make it solid because ≤
Choose a test point relative to their drawn line and shade the side that satisfies y ≤ 2x + 6. The drawn line and shading differ from the correct y ≤ −2x + 6 solution

examples.finalOutcome: The sign mistake in slope produced a different boundary and a wrong solution set

steps.title: Show Example 1 — whole class
steps.body: Put the first incorrect example on the board. Ask: "Point to the single step where this went wrong."

steps.title: Student restates the algebraic test
steps.body: One student writes the correct substitution on the board. Class confirms.

steps.title: Correct and redraw
steps.body: Rewrite the line, redraw boundary, shade correct half-plane based on the algebraic test — not intuition.

steps.title: Repeat for Examples 2 and 3
steps.body: Same routine. Each example targets a different error type — keep each group focused on their own.

steps.title: Build a 3-step checklist together
steps.body: Students summarise: (1) get boundary, (2) draw line, (3) test a point and shade where the inequality is true.

questions.title: Which single step made the solution wrong? Point to it and explain why it leads to the opposite half-plane.
How does the test-point substitution show the correct shading? Show the algebraic step.
When might slope sign be helpful — and why can it never replace the test-point check?

activity.title: Make the connections — multiple representations
activity.subtitle: Students identify which representations describe the same relationship, and explain why
activity.studentTask: Three of these four representations describe the same mathematical relationship. Which one doesn't fit — and explain how the other three connect.

representations.label: Verbal
representations.value: A line that starts below the x-axis and decreases as x increases.

teachingNotes.title: Equation, graph, table all match
teachingNotes.body: The y-intercept is 1 in all three. The constant rate of change (+2 per unit) appears as the coefficient, the slope of the line, and the consistent +2 difference in the y-column.

teachingNotes.title: Verbal is the distractor
teachingNotes.body: It says the line decreases and starts below the x-axis — both wrong. Push students past "it says the wrong thing" toward: which specific words are incorrect, and what should replace them?

teachingNotes.title: Key connection to surface
teachingNotes.body: Ask students how slope shows up differently in each matching representation. Students often see it as the same number but miss that it's a ratio in the equation, a visual steepness in the graph, and a repeated difference in the table.

activity.title: Math Hospital — Diagnose & Repair
activity.problem: Graph the solution set for y < −½x + 3
activity.problemChecklist: Plot line ✓ Dashed ✓ Slope = −½ ✓ y < → shade above ✗

steps.title: Diagnose — where did the reasoning break?
steps.ask: Point to the exact step that went wrong. What was the student thinking?
steps.response: Step 4. They used < as a direction rule ("shade above") instead of testing a point. Never verified with substitution.

steps.title: Repair — rewrite the faulty step
steps.ask: Rewrite Step 4 so it leads to the correct answer. Show the work.
steps.response: Test (0,0): Is 0 < −½(0)+3? → 0 < 3 ✓ → shade the side containing (0,0) → shade below-left.

steps.title: Generalize — write the rule that prevents this
steps.ask: Write one rule that prevents this mistake — for any inequality.
steps.response: Always test a point. Never use the inequality symbol as a shading direction.

activity.footnote: Don't skip Step 1. Students need to diagnose before the repair feels necessary. Jumping to the rule makes it another thing to memorise.

wireframeNotes: Wireframe4 and Wireframe5 are the same activity card drawn twice: W4 titles by routine name and shows a description; W5 titles by generated activity name, demotes the routine to a chip, and adds Targets / Instructional Move / Strategy Tag. The model is the union of both.
Wireframe7 and Wireframe8_Option3 are one COMPARE_THE_THINKING block in Student vs Teacher view. The student view hides verdict, isError and annotation — see `studentViewHides`. No duplicated data.
Wireframe8 Options 1–5 all sit under the same activity header, so they are activity-phase block designs, not five activities. Modelled as `phases[].blocks[]` with a `type` discriminator.
Wireframe5's second card is titled "Title" (unfilled) — kept null rather than guessed; the routine chip identifies it as My Favorite No.

Wireframe2's error chips were deduped against a single 28-student roster: "Jay U. Gageche" (option B) and "Joy U. Gageche" (option C) are one student, and Zuriel B. Agard was listed under both C and D. Buckets now sum to 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 needing support, + 13 understood, + 1 no response = 28.
Wireframe2 labels all three buckets "9 students:" regardless of chip count — treated as export lorem, not data.

Name spellings drift between the modal and the Wireframe6 group lists (Dennis D. Iglebor / Dennis O. Igiebor; Nii-Adjei A. Adjatey / Adjetey-Osekreh; Oluwafisoyo / Oluwafisayo). Normalized to the `session.roster` spelling everywhere.
Wireframe2 repeats one interpretation paragraph across options B, C and D, and one option summary across C and D — kept verbatim, but it is placeholder text in the export.
Wireframe6's group guidance says "place students into A, B, or C" but only Groups A and B are drawn. Group C has no source content.
Wireframe6's two groups span 19 students including several who answered correctly, so group membership is not a subset of `studentsNeedingSupport`.
Badge text differs across screens for the same misconception (RECOMMENDED FOCUS on W1/4/5/6/8; CORE on W2/3/8_Option5) — one `badge` field, with both spellings recorded in `badgeVariants`.

Wireframe11's rows are plan state, not pipeline output, so they live under `savedPlan`. Their activity titles (Slope Forecasting Challenge, Slope Swap Error Analysis) appear nowhere else, and the completed row's misconception ("Incorrect Slope Conversion") is not one of this week's three — hence the denormalized snapshot and null activityId.

The Wireframe2/Wireframe3 background is a later iteration of Wireframe1 showing misconceptions and next steps on one page; its two activity cards carry the same title twice (placeholder). No unique data extracted from it.
Prevalence and grouping are enums with counts behind them: W1/W4/W5 show "Some students" and "whole class"; W11 shows "Few students" and "Split class".
